keyVerseText: At the same time came to them Tatnai, governor on this side the river, and Shetharboznai, and their companions, and said thus unto them, Who hath commanded you to build this house, and to make up this wall?
rootMeaning: The word תַּתְּנַי (Tattᵉnay) is a proper name of foreign derivation, specifically Persian, reflecting its origin as the name of a Persian official. While the exact root is uncertain, scholarly analysis suggests connections to Old Persian or Avestan terms possibly related to teaching or administration. This etymological background highlights that the name is not a common noun but a title or personal name denoting authority, which enriches our understanding beyond a simple label to one indicating governance and oversight in a foreign administrative context.
usageInScripture: In Scripture, תַּתְּנַי appears consistently as the name of a Persian governor in Syria, specifically one who interacts with the Jewish community during the rebuilding of Jerusalem. The term is translated mostly as 'Tatnai' or with slight variations such as 'to them Tatnai' or 'that Tatnai,' emphasizing the person rather than a concept. Its four occurrences focus on this official’s role in questioning and overseeing the rebuilding efforts, underscoring the historical and administrative significance of the figure rather than a lexical meaning.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding תַּתְּנַי as a Persian governor who opposed the rebuilding of Jerusalem enriches our grasp of the biblical narrative’s historical reality and God’s providential sovereignty. This name represents the earthly authorities God allowed to test and challenge His people, reminding believers that God’s plans often unfold amid opposition. The presence of such a figure in the text highlights the faithfulness required to persevere under scrutiny and opposition, reflecting the broader Christian experience of standing firm in faith despite external challenges. It also points to God’s ultimate control over human rulers and events, affirming that even foreign powers serve His divine purposes.
keyVerseReflection: Ezra 5:3 introduces Tatnai as the governor who confronts the Jewish builders, asking who authorized their construction of the temple and wall. The use of the name תַּתְּנַי here personalizes the opposition, showing that this was not an abstract obstacle but a real person wielding governmental authority. Recognizing Tatnai as the Persian governor enriches the narrative by grounding the conflict in historical reality and emphasizing the tension between God’s people and worldly powers. This detail invites believers to trust in God’s sovereignty even when facing authoritative challenges.
